records.title: Share Price Versus Company Size — Mega-Cap Example
records.claim: Share price alone cannot identify total issuer size.
records.worked: FICTIONAL 100 million shares × $10 = $1 billion market cap.
records.counterexample: A company trading at $500 with only 100,000 shares has $50 million capitalization, not more than $1 billion.
records.transfer: Compute 40 million shares × $8; explain why $320 million is not corporate cash.

records.title: ETF Versus Index
records.claim: An index measures a basket; an ETF is a separately traded fund.
records.worked: FICTIONAL: index 100 to 102 represents 2% index change, not guaranteed matching ETF return.
records.counterexample: A market index value is not directly a tradable security; ETF shares incur trading spreads and costs.
records.transfer: Name differences among an ETF's NAV, market price, benchmark and the fund's prospectus.

records.title: Bid, Ask, Last, Spread, and Midpoint in a Frequently Updating Quote
records.claim: Bid, ask, last transaction, midpoint and spread describe distinct measurements.
records.worked: FICTIONAL bid $10.00, ask $10.08, last $10.03: spread=$0.08; midpoint=$10.04.
records.counterexample: Neither midpoint nor last trade is a guaranteed price for a new order.
records.transfer: Recalculate bid $19.95, ask $20.10: spread=$0.15 and midpoint=$20.025; discuss missing size.
records.learningObjective: Distinguish a quoted bid, ask and last trade; compute spread and midpoint while identifying unavailable execution evidence.
records.evidenceProcedure: Subtract bid from ask in dollars per share; divide the sum by two for midpoint. Keep the unrounded midpoint for calculations. Verify quote time, venue and size separately.
records.freshTransfer: FICTIONAL: bid $19.95, ask $20.10 and last $20.00. Calculate the spread and unrounded midpoint with units. Explain whether any of these values proves a 1,000-share execution; name the missing evidence.

records.title: Compare Quote Width Without Jumping Ahead to Liquidity Analysis
records.claim: Spread width is not by itself reliable evidence of executable depth.
records.worked: FICTIONAL spreads: $20.00/$20.05 has $0.05 width; $20.00/$20.30 has $0.30 width.
records.counterexample: A narrow spread for ten displayed shares cannot guarantee a 1,000-share fill.
records.transfer: Compare $8.40/$8.48 with $8.40/$8.56 and name unknown size, time and venue.
records.learningObjective: Compare absolute quote widths without inferring executable size or guaranteed liquidity.
records.evidenceProcedure: Compute ask minus bid for each quote in dollars per share. A comparison of widths leaves size, timestamp, venue and price impact unresolved.
records.freshTransfer: FICTIONAL: compare $8.40/$8.48 with $8.40/$8.56. Calculate each spread; then explain why neither spread establishes a 1,000-share fill and identify what evidence is missing.

records.title: Order Selection, Fills, Partial Fills, and Execution Control — Market Orders
records.claim: A market order does not guarantee the last reported execution price.
records.worked: FICTIONAL: buy 100 shares when displayed ask is $5.08 with only 20 shares; full fill at $5.08 is unproven.
records.counterexample: A past $5.00 last trade cannot promise the next 100-share buy at $5.00.
records.transfer: Describe the actual order confirmation, clock, route and size needed to verify a fill.
records.learningObjective: Explain why a market-order execution price can differ from a last trade or displayed ask.
records.evidenceProcedure: Separate the last transaction from the current quote, and the displayed quantity from the intended order quantity. Use actual execution reports to establish fills; do not manufacture missing prices.
records.freshTransfer: FICTIONAL: the last trade is $6.00; the ask is $6.08 for 25 shares; a proposed market buy is 200 shares. Identify which prices and quantities are observations and which total execution cost remains unknowable. State when NO TRADE is reasonable.

records.title: Order Selection, Fills, Partial Fills, and Execution Control — Marketable Limit Orders
records.claim: Buy limits constrain price but do not guarantee order execution.
records.worked: FICTIONAL 100-share buy limit $5.06 sees 30 offered shares at $5.06; the rest might not fill.
records.counterexample: Merely touching a buy limit in past prices does not establish that the whole order executed.
records.transfer: Compare a $6.10 buy limit against an ask of $6.08 with 10 shown shares for a 100-share order.
records.learningObjective: Apply a buy-limit price constraint while distinguishing partial execution from a guaranteed full fill.
records.evidenceProcedure: For a buy limit, compare each possible execution price with the limit; total filled quantity still requires execution evidence. A quote touch alone is insufficient.
records.freshTransfer: FICTIONAL: a 100-share buy limit is $6.10, the current ask is $6.08 for 10 shares. State the permitted execution-price boundary and whether the remaining 90 shares are guaranteed. Distinguish marketability now from a later quote change.

records.title: Stops and Invalidation — Slippage and gaps
records.claim: Stop trigger is not the guaranteed exit price.
records.worked: FICTIONAL entry $10.00, stop $9.80; 100 shares filled on exit at $9.50 lose $50, not the planned $20.
records.counterexample: Confusing a planned stop with an enforceable loss ceiling hides gap and slippage risks.
records.transfer: At $10 entry and $9.40 exit, compute 80-share loss $48, then explain the stop-price caveat.

records.title: VWAP and Moving Averages in Intraday Trading — VWAP as a session reference
records.claim: VWAP requires defined bar/tick input scope and session boundary.
records.worked: FICTIONAL HLC3 bar proxy: $9.50 at volume 100 and $10.50 at volume 200 gives (950+2100)/300=$10.1667.
records.counterexample: A bar typical-price proxy is not a tick-accurate VWAP or buy signal.
records.transfer: Use two fresh fictional bar prices $10 at 100 units and $12 at 300 units; calculate $11.50 proxy.

records.claim: Market capitalization uses a security's current per-share market price times the company's outstanding share count. A size-label threshold is a separate classification convention, not an implied fact about company quality.
records.worked: FICTIONAL: 50,000,000 outstanding shares × $4.00/share = $200,000,000 market capitalization. The numerical result alone does not establish cash on hand, float, or whether a current service labels it small-cap.
records.counterexample: A share trading at $200 with only 200,000 shares outstanding has $40 million market capitalization; a higher share price can coexist with a smaller issuer. Stale outstanding-share data makes both calculations unreliable.
records.transfer: Given a fictional 80 million outstanding shares and $7.50 current price, calculate $600 million market capitalization, then identify the original issuer evidence needed to verify the share count and its as-of date.
records.title: Market-Cap Classification — Small-Cap Example
records.evidenceScope: Verified general SEC/FINRA educational principle, not independently verified market history or individually approved full Lab.

records.claim: FINRA's new intraday-margin standards became effective June 4, 2026; firms that need additional time may implement them through October 20, 2027. A trader must check which regime their actual brokerage has implemented rather than universally applying or retiring the old pattern-day-trader minimum.
records.worked: FICTIONAL conditional exercise dated October 31, 2026: Broker A has implemented the newer intraday standards; Broker B is still within the permitted transition period and uses its earlier implementation. The same trader cannot assume either firm's specific buying-power rules without verifying its current account disclosures.
records.counterexample: Claiming that every U.S. margin account still needs $25,000 on October 31, 2026, or that none does, ignores the FINRA transition and broker-specific house requirements. Cash-account and margin-account mechanics must not be conflated.
records.transfer: Write a non-trading research checklist for a fictional October 2026 member: identify the brokerage's rule-transition notice, account type, equity, buying-power calculation, house margin and current disclosures; choose NO TRADE where these inputs are unavailable.
records.title: Accounts, Buying Power, Settlement, and Day-Trading Restrictions — Margin accounts and the 2026 transition
records.evidenceScope: Verified general SEC/FINRA educational principle, not independently verified market history or individually approved full Lab.

records.claim: EDGAR filing acceptance time does not independently establish when a filing's content became publicly available. The SEC reports typical dissemination lags of 1–3 minutes, sometimes longer, and no precise first-public-availability timestamp in the filing.
records.worked: FICTIONAL timing problem: acceptance 08:00:00 ET, independently observed public availability 08:01:30 ET, decision pause 08:00:45 ET. The later public document cannot justify an 08:00:45 inference; the observation is 45 seconds before confirmed availability.
records.counterexample: A screenshot with an 08:00:00 EDGAR acceptance stamp but no independently established dissemination evidence is insufficient to say a trader could read the filing at 08:00:00. A price move after the filing cannot prove causation.
records.transfer: Given fictional acceptance 08:03:00, independent availability 08:06:00 and decision pause 08:04:00, determine which facts were verified at the pause and write a NO TRADE or investigation decision without viewing later candles.
records.title: Verifying Catalysts, Timestamps, and Source Quality — Acceptance Time and Filing Time
records.evidenceScope: Verified general SEC/FINRA educational principle, not independently verified market history or individually approved full Lab.

records.claim: SEC EDGAR is a public original filing repository. An annual Form 10-K, quarterly Form 10-Q and event-oriented Form 8-K serve different disclosure functions; a filing alone neither guarantees accuracy of a trading thesis nor establishes event causation.
records.worked: FICTIONAL research record: Issuer A filed a 10-K for its fiscal year and a later 8-K describing a material event. Record issuer, CIK, accession, form, reporting period, amendment status, acceptance time and independently verified public availability before forming a hypothesis.
records.counterexample: A stock-news headline saying 'SEC approved the company's growth' based only on a routine filing misstates what filing means. Search-result rank, title, an amended 10-K/A, and the company's actual disclosure can differ.
records.transfer: For a hypothetical issuer reporting quarterly financials and announcing an executive change, distinguish the normal 10-Q from a possible 8-K, identify what each filing can support and list missing evidence required before a trade claim.
records.title: SEC Filings for Day Traders — EDGAR Is a Primary Research Tool
records.evidenceScope: Verified general SEC/FINRA educational principle, not independently verified market history or individually approved full Lab.

records.claim: A displayed bid and ask define the quoted price interval; the arithmetic midpoint is the mean of both prices, not a guaranteed executable price. Absolute spread divided by midpoint provides one clearly labeled relative-spread convention.
records.worked: FICTIONAL snapshot: bid $12.00, ask $12.12. Spread=$0.12/share; midpoint=($12.00+$12.12)/2=$12.06; relative spread=$0.12/$12.06×100≈0.995%. The quoted sizes, freshness, and venue remain separate evidence requirements.
records.counterexample: A narrow quoted spread with only five displayed shares cannot guarantee execution of 500 shares, and the last trade may predate the snapshot. A midpoint order can receive no fill.
records.transfer: Compute fictional bid $8.00 and ask $8.24: spread $0.24, midpoint $8.12 and relative spread ≈2.96% of midpoint; identify why size and timestamp are still necessary.
records.title: Liquidity, Spread, Slippage, and Execution Quality — Bid, Ask, Midpoint, and Spread
records.evidenceScope: SEC Investor.gov defines the bid, ask and their quoted spread. Midpoint/spread arithmetic is original fictional instruction independently checked; the source does not certify fillability.

records.claim: A displayed quote gives prospective bid and ask prices at a moment and size; a Time & Sales print is a reported transaction. Neither fact alone establishes the identity, motive or strategy of the participants.
records.worked: FICTIONAL observations: a bid of $10.00 and ask of $10.10 are observed at 09:31:00.100 ET; a $10.04 last trade timestamped 09:30:59.900 ET is earlier. That last print cannot identify the queue, participants or future executions at the later quote.
records.counterexample: A green Time & Sales row or a changing Level II ask is not proof of one particular buyer's intent or that a large displayed order executed. Feed/venue limitations and quote changes can distort simple narratives.
records.transfer: Given a fictional bid/ask at 09:31:05 and a reported $10.08 trade at 09:31:04, order the observations, calculate a $0.10 spread when bid=$10.00 and ask=$10.10, then list what the feed does not establish.
records.title: Read the Quote Before the Tape — The quote is a pair of invitations
records.evidenceScope: Verified general SEC/FINRA educational principle, not independently verified market history or individually approved full Lab.

records.claim: High reported share volume does not independently establish immediate liquidity for a particular order size. Liquidity concerns the ability to transact promptly without materially moving the price, while depth and available prices may change before an order reaches the market.
records.worked: FICTIONAL: a stock reports 100,000 shares traded in one minute, but only 300 shares are displayed at the current ask. A hypothetical incoming buy of 2,000 shares cannot assume that all 2,000 execute at that quote. A minute volume statistic is past transactions, not a current book guarantee.
records.counterexample: A 4x reported volume spike with a 40-cent spread and five displayed shares at the best ask may still be illiquid for a 500-share order. Inferring that the previous volume provides enough current ask-side depth confuses different measurements.
records.transfer: FICTIONAL: a past five-minute interval traded 90,000 shares, the current best ask shows 500 shares, and a possible buy would be 5,000 shares. Identify which 500 may be potentially available at that moment and what source/time/price evidence is missing for the rest. A NO TRADE decision is valid.
records.title: High Volume Still Requires Liquidity and Order-Size Context
records.evidenceScope: Original fictional arithmetic with SEC general educational references only; not actual corporate actions or individual full-Lab editorial approval.

records.claim: For domestic public companies, Form 10-K is generally the audited annual report, while Form 10-Q supplies unaudited quarterly statements and interim updates; the reporting period and amendments must be identified before comparing financial metrics.
records.worked: FICTIONAL: Issuer A's 2025 10-K reports full-year revenue of $80 million, while its Q1 2026 10-Q reports three-month revenue of $19 million. Comparing $19 million directly with $80 million as if both were quarterly values is invalid; a period-aligned comparison requires the prior-year three-month figure and other context.
records.counterexample: Calling a single unaudited quarterly disclosure an audited annual result—or treating a 10-K/A amendment as a second independent full-year result—can misstate the source, accounting scope, and chronology.
records.transfer: FICTIONAL: a 10-K shows annual revenue $120 million and a Q2 10-Q shows its current three-month revenue $28 million against $25 million in the comparable prior-year quarter. Compute the period-aligned $3 million or 12% change and explain why it is not directly a 28/120 growth-rate comparison.
records.title: SEC Filings for Day Traders — Forms 10-Q and 10-K
records.evidenceScope: Original fictional arithmetic with SEC general educational references only; not actual corporate actions or individual full-Lab editorial approval.

records.claim: Public securities offerings may involve registration statements and prospectuses. A proposed or registered offering is not proof that every share is already issued. If new equivalent common shares are actually issued, the ownership percentage of existing holders can decline; the filed terms and outstanding share count must be separately checked.
records.worked: FICTIONAL fully-issued simplified case: 10,000,000 common shares outstanding and 2,500,000 genuinely new equivalent shares issued produce 12,500,000 total shares. Existing holders together then hold 10,000,000/12,500,000=80% of the new total, before considering voting classes, convertibles or buybacks. This is not a verified issuer event.
records.counterexample: Announcing a shelf registration, ATM facility, warrant authorization or proposed offering does not establish that every share has already been sold or issued. Counting merely authorized shares as outstanding would manufacture dilution.
records.transfer: FICTIONAL: assume precisely 20 million identical common shares were outstanding and 5 million additional identical shares have actually been issued. Calculate 25 million new outstanding shares and a pre-issuance holder group's 80% proportion, then list what would be required to verify a real company's filing terms.
records.title: Offerings, ATM Programs, Warrants, Convertibles, and Dilution Risk — Public and Registered Direct Offerings
records.evidenceScope: SEC primary registration-disclosure generalities plus original fictional issued-share ownership arithmetic; not a claim that any real registered direct offering was completed.
